mainTopic: Praying while needing to relieve oneself, and how to handle תפילין when entering a בית הכסא
overview: The amud opens by finishing a dispute about someone who stopped in the middle of תפילה to relieve himself: does he go back to the beginning, or to where he stopped? רב אשי explains that the real question is whether the person was fit to pray at all when he started. A ברייתא teaches that one who needs to relieve himself may not pray, but only if he cannot hold himself in for the time it takes to walk a פרסה. The גמרא brings פסוקים for this, and along the way explains 'שמור רגלך' as teaching that a קרבן must come with תשובה. Next comes the topic of תפילין and the בית הכסא: they come off ארבע אמות before a regular bathroom, and they may not be worn in even just to urinate. ברייתות and a sad story explain why the תפילין are no longer left in holes outside but are held in the hand, rolled like a scroll against the heart. When there is no time left to wear them, or at night, they go in a pouch, and אביי and a proof from טומאת מת discuss its size. The amud ends with רבי יוחנן keeping his תפילין in hand but giving away his book of אגדה, and his reason continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A suggested explanation: the dispute is about how long he paused
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the two אמוראים disagree about a long pause: one says he restarts from the beginning, the other says he continues from where he stopped.
steps.simpleTranslation: One Sage holds: if he paused long enough to finish the whole תפילה, he goes back to the beginning. The other Sage holds: he goes back to the place where he stopped.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible reason why the two Sages disagree about the person who stopped his תפילה to relieve himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this suggestion, the argument is a general question about long pauses in תפילה. If the pause lasted as long as saying the whole תפילה, one view says start over and the other says continue. This suggestion is about to be rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: He goes back to the beginning
To the place where he stopped

phrases.english: One Sage holds: if he paused
phrases.notes: The two Sages are רב חסדא and רב המנונא from just before this, talking about someone who stopped in the middle of תפילה to relieve himself.

phrases.english: long enough to finish all of it
he goes back to the beginning.
And the other Sage holds: to the place where he stopped.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר סָבַר: אִם שָׁהָה כְּדֵי לִגְמוֹר אֶת כּוּלָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a suggested explanation that began before this section.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The dispute is about whether a long pause forces a restart.

steps.title: רב אשי rejects the pause explanation
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that if the argument were about pausing, the Sages would have spoken about whether he paused or not. They never mention it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: if it were about 'if he paused,' they should have mentioned 'if he did not pause'!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי pushes back against the explanation in step 1.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The original dispute says nothing about how long the person paused. If the length of the pause were the real issue, the Sages would have separated a long pause from a short one. Since they did not, the pause cannot be the point of the argument.

phrases.english: רב אשי said:
This 'if he paused'
they should have said 'if he did not pause'!

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי ״אִם שָׁהָה״, אִם לֹא שָׁהָה מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion in step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole idea that the dispute is about the length of the pause.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The original dispute never mentions pausing, so pausing cannot be what they argue about.

steps.title: The real dispute: was he fit to pray when he started?
steps.stepSummary: Everyone agrees that a long pause means starting over. They argue about a short pause: was this man unfit to pray from the start, or was he fit?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, everyone agrees that if he paused long enough to finish the whole תפילה, he goes back to the beginning. They argue when he did not pause that long. One Sage holds he was a disqualified man, not fit, so his prayer is not a prayer. The other Sage holds he was a fit man, so his prayer is a prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives his own explanation of the dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The long-pause rule is now agreed by both sides. The dispute moves to the man's status: he needed to relieve himself when he began. One view says that need made him unfit from the start, so even the first part of his תפילה does not count and he must start over. The other view says he was fit, so what he said counts and he continues from where he stopped.

keyTerms.meaning: A man who is pushed away, meaning disqualified
His prayer counts as a prayer

steps.whatToRemember: Everyone agrees a long pause means starting over. The argument is whether needing to relieve himself made the person unfit to pray from the very beginning.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the argument is still about how long he paused. Both sides now agree on that. The argument is only about the person's fitness.

phrases.english: Rather, everyone agrees

phrases.aramaic: אִם שָׁהָה כְּדֵי לִגְמוֹר אֶת כּוּלָּהּ
phrases.english: if he paused long enough to finish all of it
he goes back to the beginning,
and there, they argue about where he did not pause that long,
for one Sage holds he is a disqualified man,
phrases.notes: He needed to relieve himself before he even started, so this view treats him as unfit from the start.

phrases.english: and not fit, and his prayer is not a prayer.
And the other Sage holds he is a fit man,
and his prayer is a prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אִם שָׁהָה כְּדֵי לִגְמוֹר אֶת כּוּלָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected explanation with a new one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the dispute to a different question
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute was about the length of the pause.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dispute is about whether the man was fit to pray when he started.

steps.title: ברייתא: one who needs to relieve himself should not pray
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that someone who needs to relieve himself may not pray, and if he did, his prayer is an abomination.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: one who needs to relieve himself should not pray. If he prayed, his prayer is an abomination.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a related, strong rule about praying while needing to relieve oneself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes beyond the earlier case of stopping in the middle. Here the ברייתא forbids starting at all in that state and calls such a prayer a תועבה.

keyTerms.meaning: One who needs to relieve himself

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
one who needs to relieve himself should not pray,
phrases.notes: Literally, 'one who needs his openings,' a polite way of saying he needs the bathroom.

phrases.english: and if he prayed, his prayer is an abomination.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַנִּצְרָךְ לִנְקָבָיו — אַל יִתְפַּלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a related topic with a new source.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who needs to relieve himself should not pray; if he does, his prayer is a תועבה.

steps.title: Limit: only if he cannot hold himself in
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד, or some say רב יהודה, limits the ברייתא: it applies only when the person cannot hold himself in.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד, and some say רב יהודה, said: they only taught this when he cannot hold himself in. But if he can hold himself in, his prayer is a prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא narrows the ברייתא to one specific situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The harsh word תועבה applies only to someone with an urgent need. If he can wait comfortably, his prayer is fully valid.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical halacha: a slight need does not ruin a תפילה, but an urgent one does.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: Rav Zevid, and some say Rav Yehuda, said:
They only taught this
where he cannot hold himself in,
but if he can hold himself in,
his prayer is a prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לִשְׁהוֹת בְּעַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the ruling of step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא applies only to one who cannot hold himself in.

steps.title: How long must he be able to hold in?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what counts as being able to hold himself in.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for how long?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a measurement. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Able to hold himself in' is unclear without a time limit, so the גמרא asks how long he must be able to wait.

keyTerms.meaning: Up to how much, meaning for how long

phrases.english: And for how long?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַד כַּמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the measurement behind step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How long he must be able to hold himself in for his prayer to count.

steps.title: רב ששת: the time to walk a פרסה
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers: as long as it takes to walk a פרסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: up to a פרסה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the question with a measurement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he could hold himself in for the time it takes to walk a פרסה, he counts as able to wait, and his prayer is valid.

keyTerms.meaning: A פרסה, a unit of distance; here, the time it takes to walk it

steps.whatToRemember: The measure for 'able to hold himself in' is the time it takes to walk a פרסה.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said: up to a parasang.
phrases.notes: He means the time it takes to walk that distance.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: עַד פַּרְסָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The time it takes to walk a פרסה.

steps.title: Another version: the limit is in the ברייתא itself
steps.stepSummary: Some teach the 'can he hold himself in' limit as part of the ברייתא itself, and give the פרסה measure in the name of רב זביד.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some teach this on the ברייתא itself: When is this said? When he cannot control himself. But if he can control himself, his prayer is a prayer. And for how long? רב זביד said: up to a פרסה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of who said what in steps 5 through 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The halacha stays the same. Only the sources change. In this version the limit comes from the ברייתא, not from an אמורא, and the פרסה measure is said by רב זביד instead of רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case is this said?

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new ruling. It is the same rule with different sources: here the limit is part of the ברייתא, and רב זביד gives the פרסה measure.

phrases.english: Some teach it on the baraita:
In what case is this said?
When he cannot control himself.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אִם יָכוֹל לַעֲמוֹד עַל עַצְמוֹ
phrases.english: But if he can control himself,
his prayer is a prayer.
And for how long?
Rav Zevid said: up to a parasang.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּמַתְנֵי לַהּ אַמַּתְנִיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of steps 5 through 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא itself limits the rule to one who cannot control himself, and רב זביד sets the measure at a פרסה.

steps.title: A source from a פסוק: one who needs the bathroom may not pray
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני, quoting רבי יונתן, rules that one who needs to relieve himself may not pray, based on 'הכון לקראת אלהיך ישראל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: Someone who needs to relieve himself may not pray, because the פסוק says, 'Prepare to greet your God, Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another אמורא who states the same rule as the earlier ברייתא, and this time it gives a פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 4-8 gave the rule and how far it goes. Now we get the reason from a פסוק. Praying means coming to greet God, so you must be prepared, and a person who is pressed to use the bathroom is not prepared.

keyTerms.meaning: One who needs to relieve himself (literally, 'needs his openings')
Because it says (introduces a פסוק as the source)

steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a source in the תנ"ך for the halacha, so this rule is about showing proper respect when standing before God.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said
Rabbi Yonatan said:
One who needs to relieve himself
may not pray,
because it is said:
"Prepare to greet your God, O Israel."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק as the source for the rule of the ברייתא in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who needs to relieve himself may not pray, because a person must be prepared when greeting God.

steps.title: Reading 'Guard your foot when you go to the house of God'
steps.stepSummary: In the same chain of names, רבי יונתן explains 'שמור רגלך' as: guard yourself from sin, and if you sin, bring a קרבן before Me.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני also said in the name of רבי יונתן: What does the פסוק 'Guard your foot when you go to the house of God' mean? Guard yourself so you don't sin, and if you do sin, bring a קרבן before Me.
steps.whatsHappening: Since it just quoted these רבנים, the גמרא brings another teaching of theirs on a related פסוק about coming before God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Guard your foot' is read as 'guard yourself' from sin. The 'house of God' is the בית המקדש, the place you bring a קרבן if you did sin. This sets up the explanation of the rest of the פסוק in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: What does the פסוק mean? (opens an explanation of a פסוק)
A sacrifice brought in the בית המקדש

phrases.english: And Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said
Rabbi Yonatan said:
What is meant by that which is written:
"Guard your foot when you go
to the house of God"?
Guard yourself so that you do not sin,
and if you do sin,
bring a sacrifice before Me.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן: מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brought next because it has the same chain of names and the same theme of coming before God.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'שמור רגלך' means guard yourself from sin, and if you sin, bring a קרבן.

steps.title: רבא: be like the wise who repent, not like fools who don't
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the next part of the פסוק. Listen to the wise, who bring a קרבן and also do תשובה. Do not be like the fools, who bring a קרבן but do not do תשובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And be ready to listen to the words of the wise.' רבא said: Be close to hearing the words of the wise, because when they sin they bring a קרבן and also do תשובה. 'Rather than fools giving a sacrifice': do not be like the fools who sin and bring a קרבן but do not do תשובה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא keeps going through the same פסוק and explains its middle part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק compares two kinds of people who both bring a קרבן. The wise add real תשובה. The fools think the קרבן alone is enough, so the point is that a קרבן without תשובה is missing the main thing.
steps.whatToRemember: A קרבן works together with תשובה. Bringing a קרבן without regret is what fools do.

phrases.english: "And be near to listen to the words of the wise."
phrases.notes: This is the next part of the same פסוק. The פסוק itself just says 'be near to listen'; 'the words of the wise' is the גמרא's explanation.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Be near to listen to the words of the wise,
who, if they sin,
bring a sacrifice and repent.
"Than when fools give a sacrifice":
do not be like the fools
who sin and bring a sacrifice
but do not repent.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְקָרוֹב לִשְׁמֹעַ דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים, אָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes on to explain the next words of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wise bring a קרבן and also do תשובה. Fools bring a קרבן without תשובה.

steps.title: Challenge: if they don't know how to do evil, they are righteous
steps.stepSummary: The end of the פסוק, 'they do not know to do evil', seems to praise the fools. That cannot be right.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'For they do not know to do evil.' If so, they are righteous people!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reaches the last words of the פסוק and points out that, read simply, they don't fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The simple meaning of 'they don't know how to do evil' sounds like praise, as if these people never sin. But the פסוק just called them fools who sin without תשובה, so the plain reading cannot be correct.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a question about halacha. The גמרא is saying the simple reading of the end of the פסוק clashes with how the פסוק treats the fools, so a different reading is needed.

phrases.english: "For they do not know to do evil":
If so, they are righteous!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי צַדִּיקִים נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the plain meaning of the end of the פסוק that רבא was explaining.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain reading of 'כי אינם יודעים לעשות רע'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the fools don't know how to do evil, they would be righteous. That contradicts the פסוק calling them sinful fools.

steps.title: Reread: the fools can't tell good from bad
steps.stepSummary: The end of the פסוק means the fools don't know whether their קרבן is a thank-offering for good or an atonement for sin. God protests that people who can't tell good from bad bring Him a קרבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: do not be like the fools who sin and bring a קרבן but don't know whether they are bringing it for something good or for something bad. ה׳ said: They can't tell the difference between good and bad, and they bring a קרבן before Me?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by giving the end of the פסוק a new meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'They don't know to do evil' now means 'they don't recognize what evil is'. Because these people don't notice their sins, they cannot even tell whether their קרבן is a thank-offering or an atonement. So their קרבן is empty, and God complains about it.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He

phrases.english: Rather: do not be like the fools
who sin and bring a sacrifice
and do not know
whether they are bringing it for the good,
phrases.notes: He means a thank-offering for something good that happened.

phrases.english: or whether they are bringing it for the bad.
phrases.notes: He means an offering to make up for a sin.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
Between good and bad they cannot tell,
and they bring a sacrifice before Me?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, אַל תְּהִי כַּכְּסִילִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12 by rereading the end of the פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'They do not know to do evil' sounded like praise, as if they never sin.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means they can't recognize evil, so they don't know whether their קרבן is for good or for sin.

steps.title: Another reading: guard your body during prayer
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי (or רבי חנינא בר פפא) reads 'שמור רגלך' as: guard your body openings when you stand before Me in prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי, and some say רבי חנינא בר פפא, said: Guard your openings when you stand before Me in prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: A different אמורא gives another meaning for 'Guard your foot' that brings us back to the topic of praying when you need the bathroom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'foot' is read as a polite way of referring to the body's openings. So the פסוק becomes another source that you must keep your body under control while you pray, just like the rule in step 9.
steps.whatToRemember: Both 'הכון לקראת אלהיך' and 'שמור רגלך' teach that before praying you must make sure your body won't distract you or show disrespect.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi, and some say
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa, said:
Guard your openings
phrases.notes: He is reading 'Guard your foot' from the פסוק as a polite way of saying this.

phrases.english: at the time that you stand
in prayer before Me.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בַּר פָּפָּא אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different reading of 'שמור רגלך' from the one in step 10, and ties it back to the rule in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'שמור רגלך' means guard your body openings while praying.

steps.title: Remove תפילין ארבע אמות before a bathroom
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a person entering a bathroom takes off his תפילין at a distance of אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת and then goes in.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: someone going into a bathroom takes off his תפילין when he is still ארבע אמות away, and then he goes in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא about taking off תפילין before entering a bathroom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is simple: you may not bring תפילין into a bathroom, and you must take them off before you get close to it. The distance is אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת, not the doorway itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Four cubits, about six to eight feet

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
One who enters a bathroom
removes his tefillin at a distance of four amos
and then enters.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַנִּכְנָס לְבֵית הַכִּסֵּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new halachic topic after the aggadic reading of 'שמור רגלך' about guarding oneself during prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One must take off his תפילין אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת before entering a bathroom.

steps.title: Regular bathroom versus makeshift bathroom
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת says the rule of ארבע אמות applies only to a regular bathroom. At a makeshift spot, a person takes off the תפילין and relieves himself right away. When he leaves, he must move ארבע אמות away before putting them back on, because he has now made the spot a regular bathroom.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר רב הונא said in the name of רב ששת: the ברייתא is talking only about a regular bathroom. At a makeshift bathroom, a person takes off his תפילין and relieves himself immediately. But when he leaves, he walks ארבע אמות away and only then puts them back on, because by using the place he turned it into a regular bathroom.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא limits the ברייתא we just learned: the four-amos distance before entering applies only to a regular bathroom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A makeshift spot is not a bathroom until it is used, so there is no need to take the תפילין off four amos before it. Once he has used it, it counts as a regular bathroom. That is why he must move four amos away before putting the תפילין back on.

keyTerms.meaning: Puts them on (here: puts the תפילין back on)

steps.confusionAlert: The makeshift spot gets two different treatments. Going in, it is still not a bathroom, so no distance is needed. Coming out, it already counts as a regular bathroom, so the ארבע אמות apply.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna said in the name of Rav Sheshet:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בֵּית הַכִּסֵּא קָבוּעַ,
phrases.english: They taught this only about a regular bathroom,
but a makeshift bathroom —
he removes them and relieves himself right away.

phrases.aramaic: וּכְשֶׁהוּא יוֹצֵא — מַרְחִיק אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת, וּמַנִּיחָן,
phrases.english: And when he leaves, he moves four amos away and puts them on,
phrases.notes: Here 'puts them' means putting the תפילין back on his head and arm, not setting them down.

phrases.english: because he has made it a regular bathroom.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the ברייתא of step 15 to a regular bathroom.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The four-amos rule before entering applies only to a regular bathroom. A makeshift one becomes regular once used, so the four amos apply when leaving it.

steps.title: May one wear תפילין into a bathroom just to urinate?
steps.stepSummary: The yeshiva asks whether a person may enter a regular bathroom wearing תפילין only to urinate. רבינא permits it and רב אדא בר מתנא forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: may a person go into a regular bathroom with his תפילין on, just to urinate? רבינא allowed it, and רב אדא בר מתנא forbade it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question about urinating and shows that two אמוראים disagreed about it. This sets up the next step, where רבא will decide.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Urinating is a lighter case than relieving oneself fully, so maybe the תפילין do not need to come off. The two אמוראים split on this, and רבא settles it in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among them

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
May a person enter wearing tefillin
into a regular bathroom in order to urinate?

phrases.aramaic: רָבִינָא שָׁרֵי, רַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָא אָסַר.
phrases.english: Ravina permitted it; Rav Adda bar Masna forbade it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: מַהוּ שֶׁיִּכָּנֵס אָדָם בִּתְפִילִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the regular-bathroom rule and asks about the lighter case of only urinating.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether one may wear תפילין into a regular bathroom just to urinate.

steps.title: רבא forbids it and explains why
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that it is forbidden, because he might end up relieving himself fully with the תפילין on. Another version says the worry is that he might pass wind with them on.
steps.simpleTranslation: They came and asked רבא. He told them it is forbidden: we worry he might relieve himself while wearing them. Some say the worry is that he might pass wind while wearing them.
steps.whatsHappening: The question goes to רבא, who decides that it is forbidden. The גמרא gives two versions of his reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though he only plans to urinate, being in the bathroom could lead to something worse while the תפילין are on. The two versions agree on the ruling and differ only on which worry he had.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the rule against תפילין in a bathroom is protected with a safeguard, even when only a lighter act is planned.

phrases.english: They came and asked Rava;
he said to them: It is forbidden —
we are concerned that he may relieve himself with them on.
And some say: that he may pass wind with them on.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתוֹ שַׁיְילוּהּ לְרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17 and sides with רב אדא בר מתנא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It is forbidden, out of concern that he will relieve himself, or in another version pass wind, while wearing תפילין.

steps.title: Where to keep the תפילין while inside
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא gives three views. בית שמאי: leave them in a window near the public area. בית הלל: hold them in your hand. רבי עקיבא: hold them in your garment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: someone entering a regular bathroom takes off his תפילין four amos away, puts them in a window next to the public area, and goes in. When he comes out, he moves four amos away and puts them back on. This is the view of בית שמאי. בית הלל say he holds them in his hand and goes in. רבי עקיבא says he holds them in his garment and goes in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא that adds a new question: what does he do with the תפילין while he is inside?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees the תפילין come off. They argue only about where to keep them. בית שמאי want them left outside, while בית הלל and רבי עקיבא let him take them in held in his hand or garment.

keyTerms.meaning: Window, a niche in the wall

phrases.english: It was taught in another baraisa:
One who enters a regular bathroom
removes his tefillin at a distance of four amos,

phrases.aramaic: וּמַנִּיחָן בַּחַלּוֹן הַסָּמוּךְ לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים, וְנִכְנָס.
phrases.english: places them in the window next to the public area, and enters.

phrases.aramaic: וּכְשֶׁהוּא יוֹצֵא — מַרְחִיק אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת, וּמַנִּיחָן,
phrases.english: And when he leaves, he moves four amos away and puts them on —
these are the words of Beis Shammai.

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: אוֹחֲזָן בְּיָדוֹ, וְנִכְנָס.
phrases.english: Beis Hillel say: He holds them in his hand and enters.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: אוֹחֲזָן בְּבִגְדוֹ, וְנִכְנָס.
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says: He holds them in his garment and enters.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: הַנִּכְנָס לְבֵית הַכִּסֵּא קָבוּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the topic of the first ברייתא and adds a מחלוקת about where the תפילין are kept.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: leave them in a window by the public area. בית הלל: hold them in your hand. רבי עקיבא: hold them in your garment.

steps.title: Holding them only in the garment is risky
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to רבי עקיבא: if the תפילין are only in his garment, he may forget them and they could fall.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really think he means only in his garment? Sometimes a person forgets about them and they fall!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי עקיבא's wording, because carrying the תפילין only in a garment seems unsafe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something tucked into clothing can be forgotten and slip out, and the holy תפילין would land on a bathroom floor. So רבי עקיבא cannot mean the garment alone.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? (meaning: that can't be right)

phrases.english: In his garment — could that enter your mind?!
Sometimes he forgets about them and they fall!

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּבִגְדוֹ סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of רבי עקיבא's view in step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי עקיבא's ruling that he holds the תפילין in his garment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A garment alone is not secure. He may forget the תפילין and they may fall in the bathroom.

steps.title: Correct reading: garment and hand together
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads רבי עקיבא: he holds the תפילין in his hand, wrapped in his garment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say this: he holds them with his garment and in his hand, and goes in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question by adjusting רבי עקיבא's words so they make practical sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding them in his hand keeps him from forgetting, so they will not fall. Covering them with the garment keeps them from being exposed in the bathroom. So רבי עקיבא adds the garment on top of בית הלל's hand.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say (reread the text this way)
With his garment and in his hand

steps.whatToRemember: In a regular bathroom the תפילין come off ארבע אמות away, even if he only needs to urinate. בית שמאי leave them outside, בית הלל hold them in the hand, and רבי עקיבא holds them in the hand covered by the garment.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
He holds them with his garment and in his hand, and enters.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the קשיא of step 20 by rereading רבי עקיבא's words.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי עקיבא meant the תפילין are held in the garment alone.
steps.terutzMaskana: He holds them in his hand, covered by his garment, so they will not fall and are not exposed.

steps.title: Place them in holes by the bathroom, not by the public street
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: the person may leave his תפילין in holes next to the בית הכסא, but not in holes next to the רשות הרבים, because passersby might take them and he would come under suspicion.
steps.simpleTranslation: He puts them in holes next to the bathroom. He should not put them in holes next to the public street, because people walking by might take them, and then he would be suspected of doing something wrong.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא we have been learning keeps going. It now tells us where the person may leave his תפילין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two possible hiding places. Holes by the בית הכסא are allowed. Holes facing the רשות הרבים are not, because strangers can reach them, and losing the תפילין that way can lead to חשד (people suspecting him).

keyTerms.meaning: Holes or nooks in a wall
Passersby, people walking along the road
Suspicion, people thinking badly of someone

steps.confusionAlert: The text does not yet explain what kind of suspicion it means. The story in the next step shows exactly how it can happen.

phrases.english: And he places them in the holes next to the bathroom,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא יַנִּיחֵם בַּחוֹרִין הַסְּמוּכִים לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים,
phrases.english: but he should not place them in the holes next to the public street,
in case passersby take them,
and he will come to be suspected.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַנִּיחָם בַּחוֹרִין הַסְּמוּכִים לְבֵית הַכִּסֵּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from steps 19 and 21, explaining where the תפילין may be put down once he goes in.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Holes near the בית הכסא are allowed. Holes near the רשות הרבים are forbidden because the תפילין could be taken and he would be suspected.

steps.title: The tragic story of the student whose תפילין were taken
steps.stepSummary: A תלמיד left his תפילין in holes near the street. A זונה took them and claimed in the בית המדרש that he had given them to her as payment. Out of shame he fell from a roof and died, and the חכמים enacted that one should hold the תפילין in his garment and hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: There once was a student who put his תפילין in holes near the public street. A prostitute came and took them. She went to the study hall and said, 'Look what so-and-so gave me as my payment!' When the student heard this, he went up to the roof, fell, and died. At that time the חכמים made a rule that a person should hold his תפילין in his garment and in his hand and go in.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tells a true story that shows how dangerous it is to leave תפילין by the street. The story ends with a new תקנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story shows what the חשד from the previous step looks like in real life: the תפילין could be used as false 'proof' of a sin. Because of it, the חכמים stopped allowing the תפילין to be left anywhere outside and required holding them in the garment and the hand. This matches the reading of רבי עקיבא given in step 21.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident, a story that really happened
They enacted, made a תקנה (a new rule)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the rule about תפילין is not only about respecting them. It also protects a person's good name.

phrases.english: And there was an incident with one student

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהִנִּיחַ תְּפִילָּיו בַּחוֹרִין הַסְּמוּכִים לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים,
phrases.english: who placed his תפילין in the holes next to the public street,
and a prostitute came and took them,
and she came to the study hall and said:

phrases.aramaic: רְאוּ מַה נָּתַן לִי פְּלוֹנִי בִּשְׂכָרִי!
phrases.english: See what so-and-so gave me as my payment!
phrases.notes: She is falsely claiming he paid her for sin with his תפילין. That is the חשד from the last step.

phrases.english: When that student heard this,
he went up to the top of the roof, fell, and died.
At that time they enacted
that he should hold them in his garment and in his hand, and go in.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַעֲשֶׂה בְּתַלְמִיד אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows through a real event the danger warned about in step 22, and explains where the rule of holding them in the garment and hand came from.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After this event the חכמים required holding the תפילין in one's garment and hand when entering.

steps.title: The history of the rules: mice, then passersby, then the hand
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא tells the history. First the תפילין were left in holes by the בית הכסא, but mice took them. Then they were put in windows by the street, but passersby took them. In the end the rule became to hold them in the hand and go in.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: At first, people put their תפילין in holes next to the bathroom, and mice came and took them. So they made a rule to put them in windows next to the public street, but passersby came and took them. So they made a rule that a person holds them in his hand and goes in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא that tells, step by step, how the rule changed over time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each place had a problem. Near the בית הכסא there were mice. Near the street there were people who took things. Since neither place was safe, the only safe option left was keeping them in his own hand.
steps.confusionAlert: Step 22 allowed holes by the בית הכסא. This ברייתא says that place also turned out to have a problem, which is why the final rule became holding them in the hand.

phrases.english: Our Rabbis taught:
At first they would place the תפילין
in the holes next to the bathroom,
and mice would come and take them.
They enacted that they should place them
in the windows next to the public street;
and passersby would come and take them.
They enacted that he should hold them in his hand and go in.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: בָּרִאשׁוֹנָה הָיוּ מַנִּיחִין תְּפִילִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A separate ברייתא that lays out the whole history and ends with the same final practice: holding the תפילין in the hand.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because mice and then passersby took the תפילין, the final תקנה is to hold them in the hand when entering.

steps.title: The הלכה: roll them like a scroll and hold them by the heart
steps.stepSummary: רבי מיאשא, son of רבי יהושע בן לוי, rules that the הלכה is to roll up the תפילין like a ספר and hold them in the right hand opposite the heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מיאשא, son of רבי יהושע בן לוי, said: The הלכה is that he rolls them up like a scroll and holds them in his right hand, opposite his heart.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא now tells us exactly how to hold the תפילין in practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתות only said 'in his hand.' רבי מיאשא adds the details: roll them up neatly like a ספר, use the right hand, and hold them against the heart.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical law, how we act

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי מְיָאשָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Meyasha, son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, said:
The halakha is: he rolls them up like a kind of scroll,
and holds them in his right hand, opposite his heart.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי מְיָאשָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: הֲלָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the general rule of holding them in the hand into a precise practical הלכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Roll the תפילין like a ספר and hold them in the right hand opposite the heart.

steps.title: The strap must not hang down a טפח
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן adds a condition: the strap may not hang down a טפח or more from under the hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר מניומי said in the name of רב נחמן: This is only allowed as long as the strap does not stick out a handbreadth from under his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן adds a condition to רבי מיאשא's הלכה about how the rolled-up תפילין must be held.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rolling and holding the תפילין is only good enough if they are fully held. If a strap dangles a טפח below the hand, they are not properly held. Hanging inside a בית הכסא like that is not respectful.

keyTerms.meaning: The leather strap of the תפילין
A handbreadth, a measure of about four fingers

steps.whatToRemember: You may bring תפילין into a בית הכסא rolled up like a scroll, held in the right hand against the heart, with no strap hanging a טפח below the hand. The rule came about because leaving them outside led to mice, theft, and even shame and tragedy. The next steps add when a pouch is used instead.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Manyumi said that Rav Naḥman said:
Provided that a strap does not
stick out a handbreadth from under his hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא תְּהֵא רְצוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limiting condition to רבי מיאשא's הלכה in step 25.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Holding rolled-up תפילין in the hand is allowed only if no strap hangs a טפח below the hand.

steps.title: Holding in the hand works only when there is still time to put them on
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא limits the rule of holding rolled-up תפילין in the hand. It applies only when there is still time in the day to wear them. Otherwise one makes a pouch of a טפח and puts them in it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב בר אחא said in the name of רבי זירא: This was taught only when there is still time in the day to put them on. If there is no time left in the day to put them on, he makes a kind of pouch of a טפח for them and puts them in it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא adds a limit to the earlier rule that one rolls up the תפילין and holds them in his hand when entering the בית הכסא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding the תפילין in the hand is allowed only when he still has time to put them back on that day. Late in the day, when he will not wear them again, the hand is not enough. He must put them inside a pouch that is a טפח in size.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this when... (a phrase that narrows an earlier rule)

steps.confusionAlert: "לא שנו" does not reject the earlier rule. It only narrows it: holding in the hand is still correct, but only when there is time left to wear the תפילין.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha said
that Rabbi Zeira said:
They only taught this
phrases.notes: "This" is the rule from step 25: roll the תפילין up like a ספר and hold them in the right hand.

phrases.english: when there is time in the day to put them on,
but if there is no time in the day to put them on,

phrases.aramaic: עוֹשֶׂה לָהֶן כְּמִין כִּיס טֶפַח, וּמַנִּיחָן.
phrases.english: he makes a kind of pouch of a טפח for them, and puts them in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ שְׁהוּת בְּיוֹם לְלׇבְשָׁן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the halacha from step 25 to the case where he can still wear the תפילין that day.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Holding the תפילין in the hand applies only when there is time to wear them again. Otherwise they go into a pouch of a טפח.

steps.title: By day hold them in the hand; at night use a pouch
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן gives the same split in terms of day and night. By day, roll up the תפילין and hold them in the hand opposite the heart. At night, put them in a pouch of a טפח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: During the day he rolls them up like a ספר and holds them in his hand opposite his heart. At night he makes a kind of pouch of a טפח for them and puts them in it.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא, רבי יוחנן, states a rule that matches רבי זירא's split, this time phrased as day versus night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Day matches "time to wear them" and night matches "no time to wear them." So רבי יוחנן's ruling gives the same picture as רבי זירא's: hand during the day, pouch at night.

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
During the day he rolls them up like a scroll
and holds them in his hand opposite his heart,

phrases.aramaic: וּבַלַּיְלָה עוֹשֶׂה לָהֶן כְּמִין כִּיס טֶפַח, וּמַנִּיחָן.
phrases.english: and at night he makes a kind of pouch of a טפח for them, and puts them in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּיּוֹם גּוֹלְלָן כְּמִין סֵפֶר וּמַנִּיחָן בְּיָדוֹ כְּנֶגֶד לִבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ruling that matches רבי זירא's split between having time and not having time.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By day, rolled up in the hand opposite the heart. At night, in a pouch of a טפח.

steps.title: A container that is not their own may be smaller than a טפח
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the one-טפח size applies only to the תפילין's own regular container. In a container that is not theirs, even less than a טפח is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: They taught the one-טפח rule only for a container that is their own container. In a container that is not their own container, even less than a טפח is fine.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי narrows the "pouch of a טפח" rule from the last two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The size requirement is about the תפילין's own regular container. If he puts them in some other container that is not theirs, that container can be smaller than a טפח and still be fine.

keyTerms.meaning: A container that is their own (the תפילין's regular container)
That is not their own container

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. The תפילין's own container needs to be a טפח; a container that is not theirs may be even smaller.

phrases.english: Abaye said: They only taught this
phrases.notes: "This" is the need for a pouch of a טפח from the last two steps.

phrases.english: for a container that is their own container,
but in a container that is not their own container,
even less than a טפח is fine.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בִּכְלִי שֶׁהוּא כִּלְיָין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the pouch-of-a-טפח requirement from steps 27–28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The one-טפח size applies only to the תפילין's own container. A container that is not theirs may be smaller.

steps.title: Support from small containers in a tent with a dead body
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא, or some say רב אשי, supports אביי. Small jugs protect what is inside them in a tent with a dead body, so a container smaller than a טפח can still act as a real barrier.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא said, and some say it was רב אשי: You can see this is true, because small jugs protect what is inside them in a tent with a dead body.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support from the laws of טומאת מת to back up אביי's point that a small container can count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With טומאת מת, a space usually needs to be a טפח to block the טומאה. Yet small jugs, smaller than a טפח, still protect what is inside them. This shows a small container can be a real barrier, so a container that is not the תפילין's own may also be less than a טפח.

keyTerms.meaning: Know this / you can see it is true (a phrase that brings proof)
Protect (keep what is inside from becoming טמא)
A tent (roofed space) containing a dead body

steps.whatToRemember: Summary: holding the תפילין in the hand works when he can still wear them that day (daytime). Otherwise he needs a pouch: a טפח for their own container, or even smaller for a container that is not theirs. Small jugs in a tent with a dead body show that a small container can still be a real barrier.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra said, and some say it was Rav Ashi:
You can see this is true, because small jugs
protect what is inside them in a tent with a dead body.
phrases.notes: The jugs are smaller than a טפח, yet what is inside them stays טהור. So even a small container counts.

steps.triggerLanguage: תֵּדַע שֶׁהֲרֵי פַּכִּין קְטַנִּים מַצִּילִין בְּאֹהֶל הַמֵּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for אביי's ruling that a container that is not the תפילין's own may be smaller than a טפח.
steps.raayaObject: אביי's ruling that a container that is not the תפילין's own may be less than a טפח.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The law that small jugs protect what is inside them in a tent with a dead body.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן gave away his book of אגדה but kept his תפילין
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה reports that before entering the בית הכסא, רבי יוחנן gave his book of אגדה to his students but did not give them his תפילין. He began to explain this by saying that the רבנן had permitted it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: When we used to walk behind רבי יוחנן and he wanted to go into the bathroom, if he was holding a book of אגדה, he would give it to us. If he was holding תפילין, he would not give them to us. He said: Since the רבנן permitted them...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story about what רבי יוחנן did in real life when he had to enter a בית הכסא. He began to explain his reason, and the explanation finishes in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps taught that you may hold rolled-up תפילין in your hand when entering a בית הכסא. Here we see רבי יוחנן living by that rule: he kept the תפילין, which the רבנן had allowed, but he handed off the book of אגדה, which had no such permission. His explanation, 'since the רבנן permitted them,' is cut off here and continues next.

keyTerms.meaning: A book of אגדה: stories and non-legal teachings of חז"ל

steps.confusionAlert: Don't jump to conclusions about why he treated the two differently. His sentence 'since the רבנן permitted them' is not finished here. The rest of his reason comes on the next amud.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a great אמורא actually following the permission to hold תפילין when entering a בית הכסא, while treating a book of אגדה differently.

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲוָה אָזְלִינַן בָּתְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
phrases.english: When we would walk after Rabbi Yochanan,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲוָה בָּעֵי לְמֵיעַל לְבֵית הַכִּסֵּא
phrases.english: when he wanted to go into the bathroom,
when he was holding a book of aggada,
he would give it to us.
When he was holding tefillin,
he would not give them to us.
He said: Since the Sages permitted them,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה: כִּי הֲוָה אָזְלִינַן בָּתְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the size of the container back to the practice of holding תפילין in the hand, showing רבי יוחנן's own conduct.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may keep תפילין in hand when entering a בית הכסא because the רבנן permitted it, but a book of אגדה should be handed to someone else.
